Epicureanism is the ancient philosophical school founded by Epicurus around three hundred seven before Christ, teaching that the goal of life is pleasure, understood not as hedonistic excess but as freedom from pain and mental disturbance. Contrary to later caricature, Epicurus advocated modest living, simple food, and prudent friendship, arguing that many desires are unnecessary and that their pursuit produces suffering. For Epicureanism, intellectual and philosophical pleasures are superior to bodily ones; a life of contemplation with trusted friends in a garden is the ideal. Epicureanism shares with Stoicism the goal of tranquility but achieves it through prudent pleasure rather than duty.

Epicurus, living from three hundred forty-one to two hundred seventy before Christ, founded the school in his garden in Athens and taught that pleasure is the highest good. He was misrepresented by detractors as advocating excess, but he actually taught that most desires are harmful and unnecessary. The Epicurean ideal consists of modest living, philosophical conversation, simple food such as bread, water, and occasional cheese, and freedom from fear and pain.

Epicurean ethics and practice rest on aponia and ataraxia, the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance which are the true pleasures. Epicureans categorize desires into three kinds: natural and necessary ones like food, water, and shelter; natural but unnecessary ones like luxury foods; and vain desires like wealth and fame. Prudence in pursuing pleasure means avoiding desires that produce greater suffering; the examined life minimizes net pain. Intellectual pleasures derived from philosophy, friendship, and memory are superior to bodily ones and less dependent on external circumstance. Philosophy is practical wisdom, not abstract theory, and its goal is to liberate from fear of gods, fear of death, and fear of pain. This wisdom is captured in what Epicurus called the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure: do not fear God, do not fear death, pain is easily endured, and the good is easy to acquire.

Epicureanism was a countercultural philosophy in a hierarchical world obsessed with honor and power. By arguing that pleasure, rightly understood, is the good and that virtue serves pleasure, Epicureanism offered liberation from status anxiety and political ambition. The Epicurean community lived outside the civic hierarchy with women and slaves able to participate in philosophical conversation as equals. Church fathers later denounced Epicureanism as libertine, yet philosophers like Gassendi and Hume rehabilitated it, recognizing that Epicurus taught disciplined pleasure, not excess, and that the modern confusion of epicureanism with gluttony reflects centuries of misreading; the authentic school is austere.
